findings.summary: The caption promises ten pages but the carousel contains only seven.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ten pages of dense field notes"; the part has 7 slides ("Exit Status: The Engine Behind Every Branch" … "Loop Subshells and the case Statement").
findings.fix: Change "Ten pages of dense field notes" to "Seven pages of dense field notes" (and update the identical line in part 02's caption to match its own six pages).

findings.summary: Page 1 ends with a full `case` statement example six chapters before `case` is taught.
findings.evidence: Page 1, immediately after the "Not an if/else" callout: code block `case $1 in` / `  start) up ;;` / `  stop) down ;;` / `  restart) down; up ;;` / `esac` — `case`, `in`, `)`, `;;` and `esac` are first explained on page 7 ("Shape of a case").
findings.fix: Delete the `case` block from page 1 and move the init-script dispatch example to page 7 beside the "Shape of a case" section; if page 1 needs a closing example for exit-status chaining, use an `&&`/`||`/`!` snippet instead.

findings.summary: Page 1's last two code blocks introduce `[ ]` test operators and `(( ))` arithmetic with no definition, and the `(( ))` block silently contradicts the page's own headline.
findings.evidence: Page 1 closes with `[ 10 -gt 9 ]   # true, numeric` / `[ 10 \> 9 ]    # FALSE: '1' sorts under '9'` and `(( 0 )); echo $?   # 1  - false` / `(( 5 )); echo $?   # 0  - true`, while the page's opening heading reads "Zero Is True Here" and `-gt` is only defined on page 2, `(( ))` only on page 4 (where the "Inverted Truth" callout finally explains the reversal).
findings.fix: Remove both blocks from page 1. The numeric-vs-string comparison belongs with the operator table on page 2, and the `(( 0 ))` truthiness demo belongs directly under page 4's "Inverted Truth" callout, which is the first place the inversion is explained.

findings.summary: Page 2 opens with test operators before `[ EXPR ]` syntax exists, then re-teaches the same operators lower down.
findings.evidence: The page's first block is a headingless bullet list — "Numeric: `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge`, numbers only" / "`=` and `!=` are for strings only" — but `[ EXPR ]` is only introduced four blocks later under "Spaces Are Syntax" ("`[ EXPR ]` — spaces around `[` and `]` are mandatory"), and the string operators are then repeated in the "String and Number Tests" table (`-z STR`, `-n STR`, `STR1 = STR2`, `STR1 != STR2`).
findings.fix: Move the opening bullets after "Spaces Are Syntax" and merge them into the "String and Number Tests" table as a numeric row group, so the page runs: exit codes → `set -e` → `[ EXPR ]` syntax → string/numeric operators → file tests.

findings.summary: A `while` polling loop is used as an example on the test-operators page, four pages before loops are taught.
findings.evidence: Page 2 code block between the exit-code table and the "set -e Blind Spots" sidebox: `while ! nc -z db 5432; do sleep 1; done` / `echo 'postgres is up'` — `while`, `until` and the polling pattern are first defined on page 6, where the same `nc -z db 5432` example reappears in the "Two Directions" diagram.
findings.fix: Delete this block from page 2 (it also has no bearing on the surrounding exit-code/`set -e` material) and keep the polling example only on page 6, where `while` and `!` negation of a loop condition are actually taught.

findings.summary: Page 7 states rules about `case` patterns before the `case` statement itself is introduced on the same page.
findings.evidence: The second block on page 7 reads "A quoted pattern is literal: `\"*\"` means an asterisk" / "Otherwise patterns match the expanded word directly" / "`shopt -s extglob` adds `@(a|b) ?(x) *(x) +(x) !(x)`" — but the heading "Shape of a case" and the `case $var in ... esac` skeleton come after it, and the base glob table (`*`, `?`, `[abc]`) comes later still.
findings.fix: Move this bullet list to the end of the page, after the "Globs, Not Regex" table, so the order is: case syntax → base glob patterns → pattern quoting and extglob.

findings.summary: `read` is used as the centrepiece of two pages' worth of gotchas but is never defined anywhere in the part.
findings.evidence: Page 5: "Both stay inferior to `while IFS= read -r line`." Page 6: "`while read` consumes stdin; body commands fight for it" and the "Stdin Thieves" sidebox. Page 7 opens with `while read x; do n=$x; done < <(cmd)`. No page explains what `read` does, what `-r` suppresses, or why `IFS=` is prefixed — and the caption still promises "the single correct way to read a file line by line".
findings.fix: Either add the chapter-8 material (`while IFS= read -r line; do ...; done < file`, with `-r` and `IFS=` explained) before page 7's subshell section, or cut the page-7 `read` code and reword pages 5–6 to defer forward explicitly ("covered in the next part") rather than citing an undefined idiom as the recommended form.

findings.summary: The pipe-into-loop subshell trap shows the fix before the problem and never demonstrates the variable loss it warns about.
findings.evidence: Page 7, "Keep the Body Here": `while read x; do n=$x; done < <(cmd)  # stays` on line 1, `cmd | while read x; do n=$x; done  # subshell` on line 2 — the comments `# stays` / `# subshell` are the only evidence that anything is lost; no code prints `$n` after the loop.
findings.fix: Reverse the order and add the proof, e.g. `count=0`, `grep x f | while read l; do ((count++)); done`, `echo $count   # 0 - the loop ran in a subshell`, then show `done < <(grep x f)` printing the real count.

findings.summary: The caption advertises ten pages but the set contains seven.
findings.evidence: "Ten pages of dense field notes" while `slides` holds 7 entries (pages 1–7).
findings.fix: Change "Ten pages" to "Seven pages" (or add the missing pages).

findings.summary: `set -o pipefail` is described as reporting the first failure, but Bash returns the status of the *last* (rightmost) command that exited non-zero.
findings.evidence: "Pipeline status = LAST command; `set -o pipefail` = first failure" — Bash manual: "If set, the return value of a pipeline is the value of the last (rightmost) command to exit with a non-zero status". E.g. `set -o pipefail; (exit 3) | (exit 4); echo $?` prints 4, not 3.
findings.fix: Reword to: "Pipeline status = LAST command; `set -o pipefail` = the rightmost failing command's status (non-zero if any stage failed)."

findings.summary: The claim that `set -e` is suppressed "after `&&`, `||`" is wrong for the final command of such a list, which does still abort the script.
findings.evidence: "Suppressed after `&&`, `||` and `!`" — Bash exempts "any command executed in a `&&` or `||` list except the command following the final `&&` or `||`". `set -e; true && false; echo after` exits before printing `after`.
findings.fix: Change the bullet to "Suppressed in every part of an `&&` / `||` list except the last command — and by `!`".

findings.summary: `[ "$f" = *.txt ]` is said to compare against the literal `*.txt`, but the unquoted `*.txt` is glob-expanded by the shell before `[` ever runs.
findings.evidence: "`[ "$f" = *.txt ]` compares to the literal `*.txt`" — with any `.txt` file in the CWD the word expands to those filenames, so `[` receives extra arguments and fails with `bash: [: too many arguments`; it only stays literal when the glob matches nothing.
findings.fix: Reword to: "`[ "$f" = *.txt ]` never pattern-matches — the shell either glob-expands `*.txt` against the CWD (→ `too many arguments`) or passes it through as a literal string."

findings.summary: The "Rules of Thumb" box states left-side quoting is never needed, directly beneath a table that includes `[ ]`, where left-side quoting is mandatory.
findings.evidence: Table row "`[ ]`","yes","no","POSIX `sh`" immediately followed by sidebox item "Left side: quoting never needed" — yet page 3 shows `[ $x = a ]` erroring when `x` is empty.
findings.fix: Scope the item explicitly: "Inside `[[ ]]`: left side needs no quoting (in `[ ]` it always does)."

findings.summary: `${arr[*]}` only collapses to a single word when it is quoted; unquoted it word-splits like `${arr[@]}`.
findings.evidence: "`${arr[*]}` joins everything into one word" — unquoted, `${arr[*]}` is joined with the first char of IFS and then word-split again, so `arr=(a b); for x in ${arr[*]}` iterates twice.
findings.fix: Write "`"${arr[*]}"` joins everything into one word (unquoted, it splits like `[@]`)".

findings.summary: The for-loops page opens with a leftover arithmetic-chapter callout unrelated to its title.
findings.evidence: Page 5's first block, before any `for` content: callout "Guard Idiom" — "`if (( count > 0 )); then` reads better and is safer than `[ \"$count\" -gt 0 ]`."
findings.fix: Move this callout to the end of page 4, where `(( ))` is taught, so page 5 opens on the "Word-List Form" heading.
